{{Short description|Ideal generated by one-term polynomials}}
In [[abstract algebra]], a '''monomial ideal''' is an [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] generated by [[monomial]]s in a multivariate [[polynomial ring]] over a [[field (mathematics)|field]].

==Definitions and properties==

Let <math>\mathbb{K}</math> be a field and <math>R = \mathbb{K}[x]</math> be the polynomial ring over <math>\mathbb{K}</math> with ''n'' indeterminates <math>x = x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n</math>. 

A '''monomial''' in <math>R</math> is a product <math>x^{\alpha} = x_1^{\alpha_1} x_2^{\alpha_2} \cdots x_n^{\alpha_n}</math> for an ''n''-tuple <math>\alpha = (\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dotsc, \alpha_n) \in \mathbb{N}^n</math> of nonnegative [[integer]]s.

The following three conditions are equivalent for an ideal <math>I \subseteq R</math>:
# <math>I</math> is generated by monomials,
# If <math display="inline">f = \sum_{\alpha \in \mathbb{N}^n} c_{\alpha} x^{\alpha} \in I</math>, then <math>x^{\alpha} \in I</math>, provided that <math>c_{\alpha}</math> is nonzero.
# <math>I</math> is [[torus action|torus fixed]], i.e., given <math>(c_1, c_2, \dotsc, c_n) \in (\mathbb{K}^*)^n</math>, then <math>I</math> is fixed under the action <math>f(x_i) = c_i x_i</math> for all <math>i</math>.

We say that <math>I \subseteq \mathbb{K}[x]</math> is a '''monomial ideal''' if it satisfies any of these equivalent conditions.

Given a monomial ideal <math>I = (m_1, m_2, \dotsc, m_k)</math>, <math>f \in \mathbb{K}[x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n]</math> is in <math>I</math> [[if and only if]] every monomial term <math>f_i</math> of <math>f</math> is a multiple of one of the <math>m_j</math>.<ref name=Dummit&Foote>{{harvnb|Dummit|Foote|2004}}</ref>

'''Proof:'''
Suppose <math>I = (m_1, m_2, \dotsc, m_k)</math> and that <math>f \in \mathbb{K}[x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n]</math> is in <math>I</math>. Then <math>f = f_1m_1 + f_2m_2 + \dotsm + f_km_k</math>, for some <math>f_i \in \mathbb{K}[x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n]</math>. 

For all <math>1 \leqslant i \leqslant k</math>, we can express each <math>f_i</math> as the sum of monomials, so that <math>f</math> can be written as a sum of multiples of the <math>m_i</math>. Hence, <math>f</math> will be a sum of multiples of monomial terms for at least one of the <math>m_i</math>.

[[Converse (logic)|Converse]]ly, let <math>I = (m_1, m_2, \dotsc, m_k)</math> and let each monomial term in <math>f \in \mathbb{K} [x_1, x_2, . . . , x_n]</math> be a multiple of one of the <math>m_i</math> in <math>I</math>. Then each monomial term in <math>I</math> can be factored from each monomial in <math>f</math>. Hence <math>f</math> is of the form <math>f = c_1m_1 + c_2m_2 + \dotsm + c_km_k</math> for some <math>c_i \in \mathbb{K}[x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n]</math>, as a result <math>f \in I</math>. 

The following illustrates an example of monomial and polynomial ideals.

Let <math>I = (xyz, y^2)</math> then the polynomial <math>x^2 yz + 3xy^2</math> is in {{mvar|I}}, since each term is a multiple of an element in {{mvar|J}}, i.e., they can be rewritten as <math>x^2 yz = x(xyz)</math> and <math>3xy^2 = 3x(y^2),</math> both in {{mvar|I}}. However, if <math>J = (xz^2, y^2)</math>, then this polynomial <math>x^2 yz + 3xy^2</math> is not in {{mvar|J}}, since its terms are not multiples of elements in {{mvar|J}}.

== Monomial ideals and Young diagrams ==

Bivariate monomial ideals can be interpreted as [[Young diagram]]s. 

Let <math>I</math> be a monomial ideal in <math>I \subset k[x, y],</math> where <math>k</math> is a [[field (mathematics)|field]]. The ideal <math>I</math> has a unique minimal [[generating set of an ideal|generating set]] of  <math>I</math> of the form <math>\{x^{a_1}y^{b_1}, x^{a_2}y^{b_2},\ldots, x^{a_k}y^{b_k}\}</math>, where <math>a_1 > a_2 > \dotsm > a_k \geq 0</math> and <math>b_k > \dotsm > b_2 > b_1 \geq 0</math>. The monomials in <math>I</math> are those monomials <math>x^ay^b</math> such that there exists <math>i</math> such <math>a_i\le a</math> and <math>b_i\le b.</math><ref>{{harvnb|Miller|Sturmfels|2005}}</ref> If a monomial <math>x^ay^b</math> is represented by the point  <math>(a,b)</math> in the plane, the figure formed by the monomials in <math>I</math> is often called the ''staircase'' of <math>I,</math> because of its shape. In this figure, the minimal generators form the inner corners of a Young diagram.

The monomials not in <math>I</math> lie below the staircase, and form a [[vector space]] [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] of the [[quotient ring]] <math>k[x, y]/I</math>.

For example, consider the monomial ideal <math>I = (x^3, x^2y, y^3) \subset k[x, y].</math> The set of grid points <math>S = {\{(3, 0), (2, 1),(0, 3)}\}</math> corresponds to the minimal monomial generators <math>x^3y^0, x^2y^1, x^0y^3.</math> Then as the figure shows, the pink Young diagram consists of the monomials that are not in <math>I</math>. The points in the inner corners of the Young diagram, allow us to identify the minimal monomials <math>x^0y^3, x^2y^1, x^3y^0</math> in <math>I</math> as seen in the green boxes. Hence, <math>I = (y^3, x^2y, x^3)</math>.

[[File:Wikipic.png|thumb|A Young diagram and its connection with its monomial ideal.]]
In general, to any set of grid points, we can associate a Young diagram, so that the monomial ideal is constructed by determining the inner corners that make up the staircase diagram; likewise, given a monomial ideal, we can make up the Young diagram by looking at the <math>(a_i, b_j)</math> and representing them as the inner corners of the Young diagram. The coordinates of the inner corners would represent the powers of the minimal monomials in <math>I</math>. Thus, monomial ideals can be described by Young diagrams of partitions.

Moreover, the [[torus action|<math>(\mathbb{C}^*)^2</math>-action]] on the set of  <math>I \subset \mathbb{C}[x, y]</math> such that <math>\dim_{\mathbb{C}} \mathbb{C}[x, y]/I = n</math> as a vector space over <math>\mathbb{C}</math> has fixed points corresponding to monomial ideals only, which correspond to [[integer partition]]s of size ''n'', which are identified by Young diagrams with ''n'' boxes.

==Monomial orderings and Gröbner bases==
A '''monomial ordering''' is a well ordering <math>\geq</math> on the set of monomials such that if <math>a, m_1, m_2</math> are monomials, then <math>am_1 \geq am_2</math>.

By the [[monomial order]], we can state the following definitions for a polynomial in <math>\mathbb{K}[x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n]</math>. 

''Definition''<ref name=Dummit&Foote />

# Consider an ideal <math>I \subset \mathbb{K}[x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n]</math>, and a fixed monomial ordering. The '''leading term''' of a nonzero polynomial <math>f \in \mathbb{K}[x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n]</math>, denoted by <math>LT(f)</math> is the monomial term of maximal order in <math>f</math> and the leading term of <math>f = 0</math> is <math>0</math>.
# The '''ideal of leading terms''', denoted by <math>LT(I)</math>, is the ideal generated by the leading terms of every element in the ideal, that is, <math>LT(I) = (LT(f) \mid f\in I)</math>.
# A '''[[Gröbner basis]]''' for an ideal <math>I \subset \mathbb{K}[x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n]</math> is a finite set of generators <math>{\{g_1, g_2, \dotsc, g_s}\}</math> for <math>I</math> whose leading terms generate the ideal of all the leading terms in <math>I</math>, i.e., <math>I = (g_1, g_2, \dotsc, g_s)</math> and <math>LT(I) = (LT(g_1), LT(g_2), \dotsc, LT(g_s))</math>.

Note that <math>LT(I)</math> in general depends on the ordering used; for example, if we choose the [[lexicographical order]] on <math>\mathbb{R}[x, y]</math> subject to ''x'' > ''y'', then <math>LT(2x^3y + 9xy^5 + 19) = 2x^3y</math>, but if we take ''y'' > ''x'' then <math>LT(2x^3y + 9xy^5 + 19) = 9xy^5</math>.

In addition, monomials are present on Gröbner basis and to define the division algorithm for polynomials in several indeterminates. 

Notice that for a monomial ideal <math>I = (g_1, g_2, \dotsc, g_s) \in \mathbb{F}[x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n]</math>, the finite set of generators <math>{\{g_1, g_2, \dotsc, g_s}\}</math> is a Gröbner basis for <math>I</math>. To see this, note that any polynomial <math>f \in I</math> can be expressed as <math>f = a_1g_1 + a_2g_2 + \dotsm + a_sg_s</math> for <math>a_i \in \mathbb{F}[x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n]</math>. Then the leading term of <math>f</math> is a multiple for some <math>g_i</math>. As a result, <math>LT(I)</math> is generated by the <math>g_i</math> likewise.

Alternatively, this follows immediately from Buchberger's Criterion, since the S-polynomial of any two monomials is <math>0</math> by definition.
